articles.title: Dyslexia Eye Tracking COrpus (DECO): First- and second-language book reading in adults with dyslexia
articles.authors: Sam Boeve, Lore François, Ella Salgado Figueroa, Esperanza Badaya, Louisa Bogaerts, Nicolas Dirix
articles.abstract: Openly available eye-tracking corpora have been indispensable for the progress in psycholinguistic theories of reading. Past corpus work extensively covered typical reading in a range of languages, but left reading difficulties relatively under-documented. In this article, we present a novel corpus, the Dyslexia Eye Tracking COrpus (DECO). It includes eye-tracking data collected from 20 Dutch–English bilingual adults in higher education with a diagnosis of developmental dyslexia. They read an entire novel (almost 60,000 words), with one half presented in their first language (Dutch) and the other half in their second language (English). After each chapter the participants answered multiple reading comprehension questions. Additionally, all participants completed several measures of linguistic abilities, including vocabulary, spelling, a 1-min reading test, and a language questionnaire. This corpus is the largest of its kind and is a direct extension of the existing Ghent Eye-Tracking Corpus (GECO) of typical reading. In combination with GECO, it provides researchers with a unique resource for studying naturalistic reading in dyslexia and its intersection with bilingualism. All data and materials are available on GitHub: https://github.com/SamBoeve/Dyslexia-Eyetracking-COrpus-DECO .

articles.title: AI-Faces by Illinois: A database of AI-generated faces depicting children
articles.authors: Tim Wei-Ting Chao, Junyi Mei, Iris Tianyi Shang, Enrique Macias, Zara Mkrtychian, Danyi Zhang, Sara A. Oh, Jasmin Serrano Rodriguez, Brenda C. Straka, Michael T. Rizzo
articles.abstract: Faces serve as gateways of impression formation during human interactions and are widely used as stimuli throughout psychological research. To source these stimuli, researchers often rely on established databases of photographs of adults’ and children’s faces or public image repositories like Google Images. Although these resources have proven valuable, there are important limitations, especially for research using images of children. This manuscript introduces a novel alternative to those databases: AI-Faces by Illinois, a database of 1152 photorealistic, AI-generated images depicting child faces that is freely available for non-commercial use (OSF link to images and norming data: https://osf.io/vurm5/ ; additional GitHub repository: https://github.com/AI-Face-By-Illinois/ai-face-by-illinois.github.io ;  https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/ ). These images vary systematically by perceived age (3, 6, 10, 15 years), gender (boy, girl), race/ethnicity (Black, East Asian, Latine, Middle Eastern/North African, Native American, Pacific Islander, South Asian, White), and emotional expression (ten smiling, four angry, and four frowning images per group). Two norming studies (Study 1: N = 1261, Study 2: N = 131) revealed that adults rated the AI-generated images as equally real as the photographs of children from existing databases and perceived them in line with their prompted age, gender, race/ethnicity, and emotion. The images also elicited perceptual biases similar to those documented in research using real faces, supporting their ecological validity. This manuscript highlights the methodological advantages and new ethical considerations of using AI-generated child faces in psychological research.

articles.title: Introducing a transparent, locally usable tool for automated assessment of second language speech comprehensibility
articles.authors: Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren, Magdalena Kachlicka
articles.abstract: Comprehensibility, or listeners’ perceived ease of understanding, is a central construct in second language (L2) speech research. However, collecting comprehensibility ratings is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and hard to scale, as each new dataset typically requires recruiting listener panels and administering rating sessions. The present study introduces A-CAT, a transparent and locally usable tool for automated assessment of L2 speech comprehensibility. Unlike commercially restricted or black-box automated assessment systems, A-CAT uses a small set of theoretically motivated acoustic predictors indexing segmental, prosodic, and fluency dimensions of spontaneous speech. Across four studies, we trained the model on listener ratings of Japanese learners’ English picture descriptions, tested its performance with new speakers, examined its generalizability to oral interview speech, and evaluated its sensitivity to longitudinal change. The model showed strong agreement with human listeners in the training dataset ( r =  .75), replicated with new speakers ( r =  .74), generalized across task conditions ( r =  .74), and detected comprehensibility gains following speaking practice. A-CAT is distributed as a standalone application and can be run locally without programming knowledge or uploading speech data to external servers. The tool provides L2 speech researchers with a practical, interpretable, and privacy-conscious method for estimating comprehensibility from spontaneous speech.

articles.title: How Personal and Perceived Values Underpin Prejudice Against 24 Social Groups
articles.authors: Marina Iosifyan, Paul H. P. Hanel, Galina Arina, Lukas J. Wolf
articles.abstract: Previous research has established that values play an important role in understanding prejudice. However, without examining whether the effects of values on prejudice generalize across social groups, conclusions may be misleading from both theoretical and practical perspectives. Across three studies conducted in the UK and Russia, participants reported their prejudice toward 24 groups (e.g., scientists, the elderly, drug addicts), their own values, and the values they attributed to these groups. Perceiving groups as valuing self-transcendence and conservation was generally associated with lower prejudice, whereas perceived self-enhancement and openness values showed little effect. In contrast, personal values varied across target groups. Prejudice was generally lower when participants’ own values aligned with those they perceived in the groups, though this congruence effect did not generalize across groups. Overall, perceived values tended to generalize across outgroups, whereas personal value effects were often group-specific, refining our understanding of how values shape prejudice.

articles.title: Small N, High Stakes: Simulating Adverse Impact With Bayesian Logistic Regression Analysis and Permutation Tests
articles.authors: Patrick J. Rolwes, Karyssa A. Courey, Frederick L. Oswald, Michelle P. Martín-Raugh
articles.abstract: Organizations frequently evaluate adverse impact with rules of thumb and statistical tests that perform poorly when hiring cohorts are small, raising scientific concerns that have legal and ethical implications. To address these concerns, this study conducts Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate Bayesian logistic regression analysis and permutation tests as two new approaches to conducting adverse impact analysis under small-sample conditions. Simulations were varied across a realistic range of effect sizes, selection rates, and group sample sizes. The performance of each method was evaluated in terms of Type I error rates and statistical power. Results indicated that both Bayesian logistic regression analysis and permutation tests are viable alternatives to traditional methods under small-sample conditions. Bayesian odds-ratio rules with noninformative or weakly informative priors in particular demonstrated higher power than frequentist methods at small sample sizes, although no method reached .80 power on average. Their Type I error rates sometimes exceeded the nominal .05 level but remained well below those of the 4/5ths rule. Implications and advantages of each method are discussed in detail.

articles.title: Less Human in Herds: Social Crowding Contributes to Dehumanization
articles.authors: Xinyu Pan, Lipeng Yin, Xiaoye Zhu, Zhansheng Chen
articles.abstract: As urbanization accelerates, social crowding has become a common daily experience. However, its impact on social interactions remains insufficiently understood. Prior work has emphasized social avoidance, but crowding may also shape how people perceive others. Across five studies ( N = 773), we applied dehumanization theory to the novel context of social crowding, showing that crowding fosters dehumanization with consequences beyond avoidance. Study 1 used natural language processing to analyze over 80,000 social media posts ( N = 71,093 users), revealing a link between crowding and dehumanizing language. Study 2 confirmed this through a field study, whereas Study 3 identified social avoidance as a pathway. Study 4 showed that suppressing social avoidance weakens crowding’s impact on dehumanization. Finally, Study 5 demonstrated that dehumanization mediated the effect of crowding on aggression. These findings advance dehumanization theory and provide insights for promoting healthier social interactions in increasingly dense urban environments.

articles.title: Drinking and the Good Life: A Daily Diary Study
articles.authors: Hannah R. Hamilton, Nicholas R. Buttrick, Shigehiro Oishi
articles.abstract: Given the prevalence of social drinking among college students, understanding the association between social drinking and the good life is key to understanding how students are achieving a good life. This 14-day diary study of undergraduate drinkers ( N = 287) examined whether consuming alcohol with others (vs. alone) and time interacting with romantic partners and friends are associated with satisfaction, meaning in life, and psychological richness. Multilevel modeling suggests social drinking was associated with greater happiness, meaning, and richness that evening. Time with a romantic partner was associated with greater meaning and richness that evening, and time with casual friends was associated with richness. Multilevel structural equation modeling revealed that increases in self-expansion and belongingness and decreases in loneliness partially mediated associations between social drinking and the good life. These results suggest ways in which college students’ social (but not solitary) drinking may help students connect with others and enhance their evening.

articles.title: Keeping Score, Feeling Poor: Exchange Orientation Predicts Lower Relationship Satisfaction Through Diminished Gratitude
articles.authors: Haeyoung Gideon Park, Mustafa Anil Topal, Mariko L. Visserman, Amy Muise, Emily A. Impett
articles.abstract: Past research shows that exchange orientation—the tendency to expect direct reciprocity in relationships—predicts lower romantic relationship well-being. However, less is known about why this transactional mindset, often grounded in seemingly reasonable ideals of fairness and balance, can be detrimental. This research examined gratitude and indebtedness as key emotional processes underlying the adverse effects of exchange orientation. Across five independent studies ( N = 1,997), reduced felt gratitude consistently mediated the association between higher exchange orientation and lower romantic relationship satisfaction for both self and partner, emerging at both between- and within-person levels, cross-sectionally and longitudinally. In contrast, mediation via expressed gratitude was less consistent, and indebtedness generally failed to account for the link. These findings clarify why exchange orientation may undermine relationship well-being, identifying erosion of gratitude as a central pathway whereby individuals perceive relational benefits as running ledgers of obligations rather than spontaneous expressions of care and interdependence.

articles.title: Paternalistic Helping Toward Older Adults: Essentialist Beliefs About Aging as a Cognitive Basis and Potential Interventions
articles.authors: Zizhuo Chen, Minfan Zhu, Min Xu, Yichao Lv, Shufei Yin, Xin Zhang
articles.abstract: Paternalistic helping can undermine older adults’ autonomy. We investigated essentialist beliefs about aging (EBA), beliefs that age-related changes are inevitable and difficult to modify, as one cognitive basis. Study 1 analyzed 123,127 archival welfare projects, finding stronger essentialist and paternalistic framing in helping projects targeting older adults than in those targeting other age groups. Study 2 ( N = 239) found that EBA were associated with preferences for paternalistic helping. Study 3 ( N = 237) showed experimentally weakening EBA reduced these preferences. Two potential broader interventions complemented this age-specific manipulation. In Study 4 ( N = 231), social constructionist thinking reduced preferences for paternalistic helping through weaker EBA. In Study 5 ( N = 240), inducing awe yielded serial indirect effects through lower need for closure and weaker EBA relative to a neutral control condition, but not a positive emotion condition. The findings supported that EBA may foster paternalism and identified potential interventions.

articles.title: Speaking From the Self: How State Authenticity Increases Subjective Agency and Challenging Voice
articles.authors: Min Ju Lee, Maryam Kouchaki, Andrew Brodsky
articles.abstract: People often avoid speaking up not because they lack ideas, but because voice feels socially risky. We examine whether and how state authenticity—the feeling of alignment with one’s true self—influences challenging voice. Across five experimental studies (four preregistered) spanning field and laboratory samples ( N = 2,195), we manipulate state authenticity and test its relationship with challenging voice. Findings suggest that state authenticity can facilitate challenging voice, with effects emerging either directly or indirectly through increased subjective agency. The agency pathway remained evident when self-presentational concern was modeled simultaneously (Study 3b) and was stronger among individuals lower in extraversion, higher in agreeableness, and higher in dispositional authenticity (Study 4). Drawing on self-determination and self-transcendence perspectives, we argue that authentic states can shift regulation toward internally endorsed action, helping individuals act on their convictions despite interpersonal risk. These findings clarify how and for whom authenticity translates into challenging interpersonal communication.

articles.title: Registered Report: Does the Relationship Between Intellectual Humility and Argument Quality Sensitivity Depend on Motivation and Cognitive Capacity?
articles.authors: Julia Lombard, Irmak Olcaysoy Okten
articles.abstract: Intellectual humility (IH) has been linked to analytical thinking and the ability to distinguish strong from weak arguments, known as argument quality sensitivity. However, it remains unclear whether this association reflects motivational factors, cognitive capacity, or both. Using an argument evaluation paradigm adapted from the persuasion literature, we experimentally manipulated participants’ motivation and cognitive capacity to examine when IH predicts argument quality sensitivity. Consistent with previous research, IH was associated with greater sensitivity to argument quality, such that individuals higher in IH more effectively differentiated strong from weak arguments. Contrary to expectations, the experimental manipulations did not reliably influence argument quality sensitivity, limiting conclusions about the processes underlying this relationship. Furthermore, the association between IH and argument quality sensitivity did not vary across motivation or cognitive capacity conditions. These findings replicate prior work while highlighting the need for stronger tests of the mechanisms linking IH to argument evaluation.

articles.title: Moral Motive Attributions Drive Desires for Dialogue Over Punishment
articles.authors: Raihan Alam, Tage S. Rai
articles.abstract: In five experiments, we examined the motives people ascribe in cases of harm and their consequences for conflict resolution. In Experiments 1A and 1B ( N = 935), participants recalled their own harmful acts as morally motivated, but harm done to them as anti-socially motivated. In Experiment 2 ( N = 681), participants preferred dialogue over punishment when offenders were morally motivated. This effect was partially mediated by perceptions that moralistic offenders possess greater moral character and are more receptive to dialogue. In Experiment 3 ( N = 534), participants were more likely to assume they had transgressed, improve their behavior, and refrain from retaliation when punishers were morally motivated. In Experiment 4 ( N = 506), choosing dialogue over punishment reduced third-party perceptions of victims’ anger, disapproval, and harm, without affecting perceptions of offenders. Moral motive attributions thus shape preferences for dialogue or punishment, responses to punishment, and perceptions of victims and offenders.

articles.title: The Existential Function of Spiritual Yearning
articles.authors: Daryl R. Van Tongeren, Patty Van Cappellen, Joshua A. Wilt, Julie J. Exline
articles.abstract: Humans seek to address existential concerns and strive for equanimity in light of potential threats. Across the (non)religious spectrum, people long for existential comfort and satisfaction—namely, they experience spiritual yearning. Across five studies (i.e., four experiments, one longitudinal study; N = 5,791), we examined the existential functions of spiritual yearning. Studies 1 to 3 ( n = 462, n = 922, n = 988) revealed that threats to meaning led to greater reported spiritual yearning to the degree people felt existentially insecure. Study 4 ( n = 424) demonstrated longitudinally how spiritual yearning was affected by the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election. To clarify inconsistent small effects, an internal mini-meta-analysis revealed a modest yet significant effect of existential threats on spiritual yearning. Study 5 ( n = 2,995) provided evidence that fulfilled spiritual yearnings enhance existential security, whereas unfulfilled yearnings undermine security. Spiritual yearning may serve existential functions.

articles.title: Social Influence in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Preference for Humans Does Not Deter Artificial Intelligence Influence
articles.authors: Constanza Musso, Andreas Kappes
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a source of social influence. But people often prefer human over AI sources (algorithm aversion/preference for humans), which might prevent AI from influencing humans. However, we outline a theoretical framework that suggests that preferences do not play a causal role in influence. To test this framework, we investigated under which conditions preferences predict AI influence. Participants ( N = 1,254) indicated their adviser preference and then made incentivised decisions while receiving advice from AI or human advisers. Participants preferred human over AI advisers but were influenced by AI and humans similarly. A strong aversion to AI advisers had no (Study 1) or a trivial relation (Study 2 and 3) with AI influence, which was explained by confounding variables. When manipulated, preferences did not predict advice-taking, but adviser trustworthiness and competence did (Study 3). Our results suggest that for predicting AI influence, understanding domain-specific social cognitions, not preferences, is critical.

articles.title: Evaluating the Ecological Validity and Mechanism of a Generative Model-Based Decomposition of Affective Variability
articles.authors: Ryan Yan Yan, Don Chamith Halahakoon, Michael Browning
articles.abstract: Affective variability is a pervasive phenomenon with important implications for cognition, behavior, and well-being. Yet the broad concept of variability may conflate distinct processes, such as transient fluctuations versus more sustained shifts. Computational approaches like reinforcement learning (RL) offer a mechanistic framework for these processes, but they are often studied in artificial settings, raising questions about ecological validity. We combined an RL task with real-world experience sampling from 332 adult Prolific participants. Using a Bayesian filter, we decomposed affective variability into short-lived affective noise and longer-term affective volatility . In the RL task, noise was driven by recent outcomes, whereas volatility reflected more distant ones. Notably, task-based noise and volatility selectively mapped onto their real-world experience-sampling method (ESM) counterparts, whereas conventional measures did not show such specificity. These findings provide a mechanistic account of distinct timescales underlying affective variability and demonstrate the ecological validity of laboratory tasks for studying real-world affect dynamics.

articles.title: Movies’ Content Features Predict the Personalities of Their Fans
articles.authors: Gideon Nave, Peter J. Rentfrow, Sudeep Bhatia
articles.abstract: Movies are a central form of entertainment and cultural expression, yet little is known about how their content aligns with the psychological traits of their audiences. We link movie characteristics and contents with the aggregate Big Five personalities of social-media users from a large, international sample who “liked” them. Movie content, captured by text keywords, predicts aggregate audience personalities beyond genre, demographics, and attributes like quality and popularity. An online experiment ( N = 1,018 adults) demonstrates that these content-based personality predictions are behaviorally relevant for choices and evaluations involving new movies and participants. We further provide fine-grained mappings between personality and movie features, including quality, popularity, genre, psychological themes, and unique concepts. Our findings reveal systematic links between personality and movie preferences, showing that people favor content that resonates with their thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. This research enables scalable, automated audience psychographic assessment based on content features, offering insights into personality-driven media preferences.

articles.title: Commentary: Abortion Attitudes and Laws Are About Gender Beliefs and Gender Inequality
articles.authors: P. J. Henry, Kate Hawks
articles.abstract: Brandt and Maner’s (2024) article in Psychological Science linked opposition to abortion with evolutionary pressures arising from high-mortality environments. Extending their analysis, we argue that such approaches overlook the critical role of gender beliefs and gender inequality in understanding abortion attitudes and laws. Using cross-national data and reproducing Brandt and Maner’s methodology, we show that when controlling for indices of gender inequality and gender-role beliefs, the previously observed relationship between mortality risk and abortion restrictiveness disappears. These results suggest that attitudes and laws concerning abortion are more robustly related to gender, rather than to ecological imperatives. We discuss the implications for evolutionary theory, gender equality, and public policy.

articles.title: Grit, Big Five Traits, and Perceived Relevance of Tertiary Music Education on Self-Appraised Career Readiness Among Music-Major Students and Working Graduates
articles.authors: Hao Yi Ho, Yu Guo Wang, Xiao Xi Tee, I Ta Wang, Fung Ying Loo
articles.abstract: This study examined the impacts of grit, Big Five personality traits, and perceived relevance of tertiary music education (PRTME) on self-appraised career readiness (SACR) among music-major students and working graduates. A total of 510 students and 250 working graduates from tertiary music education institutions in Malaysia and China voluntarily participated in the online survey. Using structural equation modeling, 63.2% of the variance in SACR was accounted for among students and 58.7% among working graduates. Following psychometric validation of the newly developed scales, PRTME significantly predicted SACR overall. For grit, only perseverance of effort (PE), but not consistency of interests, predicted SACR overall and PRTME among students. PRTME mediated the effects of agreeableness and PE on SACR in students, but not in working graduates, whereas PE mediated the effects of conscientiousness and open-mindedness on SACR overall. Significant differences were found between students and working graduates and between Malaysian and Chinese samples across several constructs, with interaction effects suggesting that these differences varied across regions. Adjusted structural models were subsequently specified to refine the significant pathways. The findings highlight the value of cultivating personality and career-relevant attributes within tertiary music education institutions to effectively enhance music-major students’ readiness for professional music careers.

articles.title: Music Characteristics and Preferences Among Older Patients Undergoing Hip Fracture Surgery
articles.authors: Antonia S. Becker, Emy S. van der Valk Bouman, Thomas L. A. Dirven, Isabel Berger, Johannes Jeekel, Markus Klimek
articles.abstract: Listening to music can reduce perioperative complications such as pain, anxiety, stress, sleep disturbances, and delirium. Currently, it is unclear how specific music characteristics influence its effectiveness and how to offer music practically in clinical settings. This study aimed to investigate the music characteristics that older hospitalized patients undergoing hip fracture surgery listened to. It is a sub-study of a multicenter randomized controlled trial on the effect of perioperative music on postoperative delirium. Patients listened to predefined playlists or completely self-selected music. Audio features and genres were extracted via the Spotify ® application programming interface, resulting in 3,195 tracks from 54 patients. Patients predominantly listened to Classical, Rock, and Pop music, with lower danceability, energy, and tempo but higher acousticness and instrumentalness compared to general music. The music matched participants’ self-reported genre preferences in 58.7% of cases. While 37.1% of participants listened to predefined playlists, 62.9% selected their own music. The latter was associated with higher self-reported music importance using binary multilevel regression and consisted of more “uplifting” audio features than the predefined playlists. Overall, preferences varied greatly among individuals. Offering a wide range of music, along with predefined playlists, seems optimal in perioperative care, emphasizing the need for personalized approaches.

articles.title: Perfectionism, Burnout, and Self-Compassion Among Undergraduate Music Majors: A Mediation Analysis
articles.authors: D. Gregory Springer, Jessica Nápoles, Mark Montemayor, Brian A. Silvey, Ethan L. Murphy
articles.abstract: Collegiate students experience a variety of stressors that affect their mental health. Music majors may be especially susceptible to these stressors because of the competitive nature of music study, students’ heavy course load, and demanding practice expectations. The purpose of this study was to explore the relationships among perfectionism, burnout, and self-compassion with undergraduate music majors. Participants ( N = 482) completed a demographic questionnaire, the Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale–Brief, the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form, and the Maslach Burnout Inventory–General Survey for Students. Participants’ scores indicated higher levels of striving than evaluative concerns on the perfectionism measure. Among the six dimensions of self-compassion, participants scored highest on mindfulness, followed by more moderate levels of common humanity, self-kindness, and self-judgment. Isolation and over-identification scores were in the low range. Regarding constructs related to burnout, participants reported not only high levels of exhaustion and moderate levels of cynicism but also high levels of professional efficacy. The results of a mediation analysis indicated that self-compassion partially mediated the relationship between maladaptive perfectionism (evaluative concerns) and burnout. Implications and suggestions for future research are discussed.

articles.title: Rhythm or Blues: The Effects of Arousing Versus Calming Music on the Sundowning Symptoms of Long-Term Care Patients With Dementia
articles.authors: Tonya R. Bergeson, Tara T. Lineweaver, Madison G. Sedlock, Kayleigh Colleary, Bradyn Swanson, Nicole A. Hagen, Marissa J. Ward, Monica G. Williams, Timothy Brimmer
articles.abstract: We examined the effects of arousing versus calming music on positive behavioral reactions and sundowning symptoms of adults diagnosed with dementia. Fifty-two patients experienced at least three sessions each of individual music listening to a playlist of calming Top 40 hits from the years they were 15 to 24 years old and individual music listening to a playlist of arousing Top 40 songs from the same years. The two types of playlists were alternated after an initial randomization as to which was first. Patients demonstrated a different pattern of behavioral reactions to the two music types, but sundowning symptoms improved similarly regardless of music type; disengagement, repetitiveness, and confusion decreased significantly at the conclusion of the music-listening sessions. The results indicate that calming and arousing music could be tailored to specific social contexts when particular types of behavioral reactions may be most helpful without sacrificing the benefits music listening offers toward reducing sundowning symptoms.

articles.title: The Spanish Adaptation and Validation of the Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index
articles.authors: Carmen Machuca-Ramos, Juan Lupiáñez, Rafael Román-Caballero
articles.abstract: The Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index (Gold-MSI) measures a wide range of musical skills and behaviors in the general adult population, regardless of formal training or musical expertise. Although the inventory has been translated and validated in multiple languages, a Spanish version is lacking. This study presents the Spanish adaptation and validation of the Gold-MSI, based on a preregistered protocol and a sample of 539 Spanish-speaking adults. Participants completed the translated inventory alongside sociodemographic and personality measures, with a subsample ( n = 250) completing a retest. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original bifactor structure, with fit indices closely matching previous validations. Internal consistency (α ~ .80) and test–retest reliability ( r ~ .85) were high for most subscales and the general factor. The Gold-MSI effectively distinguished individuals with extensive musical training and expertise from those with limited or no training. Musical sophistication was positively associated with openness to experience, extraversion, and, among younger participants, with family socioeconomic status. The Spanish Gold-MSI demonstrated strong psychometric properties, supporting its use in Spanish-speaking populations and enabling future cross-cultural research on musical behavior.

articles.title: Educational Satisfaction and Mental Health Among Classical Music Students in Higher Music Education
articles.authors: Judit Váradi
articles.abstract: Higher music education occupies a distinct position within the university system. Students pursuing classical music are required to engage in continuous individual practice and perform regularly on stage. These high expectations, competitive environments, and ongoing feedback processes can have a considerable impact on students’ mental health and their satisfaction with the educational experience. The present study explores the factors influencing satisfaction with education and the learning-support environment and examines their associations with various dimensions of mental well-being. We conducted a survey among 127 university students majoring in classical music, assessing the challenges they face during their studies and their satisfaction with teaching quality. Three satisfaction factors emerged from exploratory factor analysis: Student Community & Infrastructure, Academic & Professional Support, and Instrumental Resources. Students reported the highest satisfaction with teaching quality and the lowest with non-academic services such as sports and entertainment. Significant positive associations were found between satisfaction factors and key Mental Health Test dimensions, particularly well-being, savoring, and creative–executive functioning. Our findings provide insights that may contribute to the development of educational strategies and institutional practices in higher music education that actively support students’ mental well-being, with implications for international academic and pedagogical contexts.

articles.title: Melodic Expectancy Crossmodally Biases Social Judgement
articles.authors: Joydeep Bhattacharya, Darragh Kevin Lynch
articles.abstract: Musical expectation is one important mechanism through which music shapes emotional experience. However, the transient nature of emotions induced by musical expectancy and their potential to crossmodally influence non-auditory perceptions remain poorly understood. Across three experiments ( N = 55), we demonstrate that musically induced pitch expectations can dynamically bias social judgement of concurrently presented visual stimuli. Participants rated neutral faces as more socially approachable when paired with expected versus unexpected notes. A recognition memory experiment ruled out memory-based processing fluency accounts. Expected notes were also rated as more pleasant, confirming a subjective valence difference associated with expectancy; however, pleasantness did not significantly mediate the crossmodal effect, suggesting that the present data do not provide clear evidence that expectancy-related influences on social judgement are fully explained by explicitly reported subjective valence. These findings, which generalise across musicians and non-musicians, support the affect-as-information framework and highlight the role of predictive mechanisms in shaping emotion and evaluative judgement across sensory modalities.

articles.title: Parents’ views about teens and tech: Parents have more to gain from a trust-based digital mindset versus one driven by fear.
articles.authors: Netta Weinstein, Andrew K. Przybylski, Nicole Legate
